cards.front: Derivative
cards.back: A contract that derives its value from an underlying asset such as a stock, stock index, interest rate, foreign currency, or commodity. Options are derivatives; futures are derivatives but are not classified as securities.

cards.front: What are the rights and obligations of the buyer vs. the seller of an options contract?
cards.back: The buyer (long/holder/owner) pays the premium and has the RIGHT to exercise. The seller (short/writer) receives the premium and has the OBLIGATION to perform if the buyer exercises.

cards.front: Identify the market attitude (bullish or bearish) for each of the four basic option positions.
cards.back: Long call = bullish; Short call = bearish; Long put = bearish; Short put = bullish.

cards.front: When is a call option in the money, at the money, and out of the money?
cards.back: In the money: market price ABOVE strike. At the money: market price EQUALS strike. Out of the money: market price BELOW strike. (Buyers want ITM; writers want ATM/OTM.)

cards.front: When is a put option in the money, at the money, and out of the money?
cards.back: In the money: market price BELOW strike. At the money: market price EQUALS strike. Out of the money: market price ABOVE strike. (Buyers want ITM; writers want ATM/OTM.)

cards.front: Intrinsic value of an option
cards.back: The amount by which an option is in the money. Intrinsic value is never negative — ATM and OTM options have an intrinsic value of zero. Calls: market – strike (if positive). Puts: strike – market (if positive).

cards.front: Parity (options)
cards.back: An option is trading at parity when its premium equals its intrinsic value (i.e., time value = 0).

cards.front: What two factors determine the time value portion of an option's premium?
cards.back: (1) Time remaining until expiration — more time = more time value. (2) Volatility of the underlying — higher volatility = more time value. Formula: Intrinsic Value + Time Value = Premium.

cards.front: A customer is long 1 XYZ Jul 40 call at 3. Calculate breakeven, maximum gain, and maximum loss.
cards.back: BE = strike + premium = 40 + 3 = 43. Maximum gain = unlimited (stock can rise without limit). Maximum loss = premium paid = $300.

cards.front: A customer is short 1 XYZ Jul 40 call at 3. Calculate breakeven, maximum gain, and maximum loss.
cards.back: BE = strike + premium = 43. Maximum gain = premium received = $300. Maximum loss = unlimited (writer may have to buy stock at any price to deliver at 40).

cards.front: A customer is long 1 XYZ Jul 40 put at 3. Calculate breakeven, maximum gain, and maximum loss.
cards.back: BE = strike – premium = 40 – 3 = 37. Maximum gain = BE × 100 = $3,700 (stock can fall only to 0). Maximum loss = premium paid = $300.

cards.front: A customer is short 1 XYZ Jul 40 put at 3. Calculate breakeven, maximum gain, and maximum loss.
cards.back: BE = strike – premium = 37. Maximum gain = premium received = $300. Maximum loss = (strike – premium) × 100 = $3,700 (stock falls to 0).

cards.front: An investor is long 1 Aug XYZ 30 put; XYZ is trading at 25. State the moneyness and intrinsic value.
cards.back: The put is IN the money by 5 points (strike 30 – market 25). Intrinsic value = $500.

cards.front: How do index options differ from equity options in contract size, exercise/settlement, and trading hours?
cards.back: Index options use a $100 multiplier (premium × 100, strike × 100). Exercise settles in CASH (intrinsic value) the next business day. Broad-based index options trade until 4:15 pm ET; narrow-based until 4:00 pm ET. Expire third Friday of expiration month.

How are yield-based (interest rate) options quoted and exercised?
cards.back: Based on yields of T-bills, T-notes, and T-bonds. A strike of 35 = 3.5% yield; each full 1% movement = $1,000. All yield-based options are European-style exercise (exercisable only on expiration day).

cards.front: Trade EPIC — what currency option strategy fits an exporter vs. an importer?
cards.back: Exporters buy Puts (worried foreign currency will drop before they get paid). Importers buy Calls (worried foreign currency will rise before they must pay). All listed foreign currency options are European-style exercise.

cards.front: Differentiate American-style vs. European-style exercise.
cards.back: American-style: exercisable any time before expiration — applies to nearly all equity and equity index options. European-style: exercisable only on expiration day — applies to foreign currency and yield-based options.

cards.front: How does an investor hedge a long stock position with a protective put, and what is the breakeven?
cards.back: Buy a put on the owned stock — locks in a minimum sale price = put strike. The put gains value if the stock falls. Breakeven = stock purchase price + premium paid.

cards.front: How does an investor hedge a short stock position with a protective call, and what is the breakeven?
cards.back: Buy a call against the short — locks in a maximum repurchase price = call strike. Breakeven = short sale price – premium paid.

cards.front: Why is writing a naked (uncovered) call considered to have unlimited risk, while writing a naked put does not?
cards.back: A naked call writer must deliver stock at the strike if exercised; the stock's market price could rise without limit, so loss is theoretically unlimited. A naked put writer must buy stock at the strike if exercised; the stock can fall only to zero, so maximum loss = (strike – premium) × 100 — large but finite.

cards.front: A customer is long 100 shares of XYZ at $40 and writes 1 XYZ Jul 45 call at 3. What is the breakeven on the position?
cards.back: Breakeven on a covered call = stock cost – premium received = $40 – $3 = $37. The position is covered because the writer already owns the deliverable shares.

cards.front: List the procedural steps to open an options account at a broker-dealer.
cards.back: (1) Rep determines options are suitable; (2) deliver the OCC Options Disclosure Document (ODD) at or before account approval; (3) Registered Options Principal (ROP) approves the account; (4) trading may begin immediately upon approval; (5) customer must return signed options agreement within 15 days of approval. If not returned in 15 days, only closing transactions are permitted.

cards.front: What is the role of the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)?
cards.back: The OCC issues, standardizes, and guarantees performance of listed options contracts. It sets contract specifications (strikes, expirations), processes exercise notices, and randomly assigns them to short broker-dealers.

cards.front: When do listed options trades and equity option exercises settle?
cards.back: Options trade settlement (premium): next business day (T+1). Exercise of an equity option that delivers stock: T+1 (aligned with equity settlement as of 5/28/2024). Index option exercise: cash, next business day.

cards.front: What is automatic exercise at expiration?
cards.back: Any listed option that is in the money by at least $0.01 at expiration is automatically exercised for the holder by the OCC, unless the holder submits 'do not exercise' instructions.

cards.front: A customer buys 1 put on Napa Valley Spirits with a $50 strike and a $4.50 premium. What did the customer pay for the contract?
cards.back: $4.50 × 100 shares = $450. (Premium paid is separate from any later exercise — exercise would require delivering stock at $50.)

cards.front: What is the most appropriate options hedge for a customer who is long 1,000 shares of a stock?
cards.back: Buy 10 put contracts on that stock (protective puts) — each contract covers 100 shares, locking in a minimum sale price equal to the strike.

cards.front: What is the VIX, and what do high readings indicate?
cards.back: The VIX (Volatility Index) measures the implied volatility of S&P 500 Index options on the CBOE — the 'fear gauge.' High readings indicate the market expects greater volatility, generally leading to higher option premiums. High VIX is neither inherently bullish nor bearish.
